q: For a chemical reaction, the enthalpy change is independent of
question: For a chemical reaction, the enthalpy change is independent of
options: the physical states of the reactants and products.
the chemical nature of the reactants and products.
the various intermediate stages through which the reaction occurs.
the enthalpy values of the system at the beginning and at the end.
solution:
The enthalpy change of a reaction does not depend upon

\boxed{\text{Option C: different intermediate steps in the reaction}}

Enthalpy is a state function. This means its change depends only on the initial state and final state of the system.

For a reaction,

\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}

So, enthalpy change depends on:

  • the state of reactants and products, like solid, liquid, gas or aqueous

  • the nature of reactants and products

  • the initial and final enthalpy values of the system

But it does not depend on the path followed by the reaction or the different intermediate steps.

This is also the basis of Hess’s law. Hence, the correct answer is:

\boxed{\text{Option C}}

q: For methane(g), the enthalpy change for formation at constant pressure is $-18,500$ cal/mol at $27^{\circ}C$. What will be the corresponding enthalpy of formation at constant volume?
question: For methane(g), the enthalpy change for formation at constant pressure is $-18,500$ cal/mol at $27^{\circ}C$. What will be the corresponding enthalpy of formation at constant volume?
solution:
We are given the enthalpy of formation of methane at constant pressure ($\Delta H$), and we need to find the enthalpy of formation at constant volume ($\Delta E$).

\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l);}

Notice that water here is in liquid form, not gas. This matters because we only count moles of gaseous substances when calculating the change in gas moles.

On the product side, we have 1 mole of gas ($CO_2$). Water is liquid, so it doesn't count.

On the reactant side, we have 1 mole of $CH_4$ gas plus 2 moles of $O_2$ gas, giving a total of 3 moles of gas.

So the change in number of gas moles, $\Delta n_g$, is:

\Delta n_g = \text{moles of gas in products} - \text{moles of gas in reactants} = 1 - 3 = -2

Now we use the relation connecting $\Delta H$ (enthalpy at constant pressure) and $\Delta E$ (energy at constant volume):

\Delta H = \Delta E + \Delta n_g RT

\Delta E = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT

\Delta E = (-18500) - (-2) \times 2 \times 300

\Delta E = -18500 + 1200 = -17300\,\mathrm{cal/mol}

So, the enthalpy of formation of methane at constant volume comes out to be $-17300$ cal/mol.

q:
Identify the reactions in which, at constant pressure, work is done by the surroundings on the system:

I. 4NH3 (g) + 7O2 (g) → 4NO2 (g) + 6H2O (g)

II. CO (g) + 2H2 (g) → CH3OH (l)

III. C (s, graphite) + H2O (g) → CO (g) + H2 (g)

IV. H2O (s) → H2O (l)
question:
Identify the reactions in which, at constant pressure, work is done by the surroundings on the system:

I. 4NH3 (g) + 7O2 (g) → 4NO2 (g) + 6H2O (g)

II. CO (g) + 2H2 (g) → CH3OH (l)

III. C (s, graphite) + H2O (g) → CO (g) + H2 (g)

IV. H2O (s) → H2O (l)
solution:
At constant pressure, the work done on the system is given by

w = -P\Delta V = -\Delta n_g RT

So the surroundings do work on the system when the gas moles decrease, i.e. $\Delta n_g \lt 0$. This makes $w$ positive (work done on system).

Reaction I: $4NH_3(g) + 7O_2(g) \rightarrow 4NO_2(g) + 6H_2O(g)$

$\Delta n_g = (4+6) - (4+7) = 10 - 11 = -1$

Gas moles decrease, so surroundings do work on the system. ✓

Reaction II: $CO(g) + 2H_2(g) \rightarrow CH_3OH(l)$

$\Delta n_g = 0 - (1+2) = -3$

Gas moles decrease, so surroundings do work on the system. ✓

Reaction III: $C(s) + H_2O(g) \rightarrow CO(g) + H_2(g)$

$\Delta n_g = (1+1) - 1 = +1$

Gas moles increase, so system does work on the surroundings. ✗

Reaction IV: $H_2O(s) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$

When ice melts, volume slightly decreases (ice is less dense than water), so $\Delta V \lt 0$. This means surroundings do work on the system. ✓

So the reactions where the surroundings do work on the system are I, II and IV.

The correct option is D: I, II and IV.

q: The heat released on complete combustion of sucrose ($C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$) is 1350 kcal/mol. What amount of heat will be given out when 17.1 g of sucrose is burnt?
question: The heat released on complete combustion of sucrose ($C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$) is 1350 kcal/mol. What amount of heat will be given out when 17.1 g of sucrose is burnt?
solution:
The molar mass of sucrose $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$ is

M = 12(12) + 22(1) + 11(16) = 144 + 22 + 176 = 342 \text{ g/mol}

So 1 mole (342 g) of sucrose gives 1350 kcal of heat on combustion.

For 17.1 g of sucrose, the number of moles is

n = \frac{17.1}{342} = 0.05 \text{ mol}

Heat liberated will be

Q = 0.05 \times 1350 = 67.5 \text{ kcal}

So the correct answer is Option A: 67.5 kcal.

q:
Determine the lattice energy for the following reaction

Li+(g) + Cl−(g) → LiCl(s)

The given data are:

ΔHsub(Li) = 160 ; ΔHdiss(Cl2) = 244 ; IP(Li) = 520 ;

EA(Cl) = 365 and ΔHf(LiCl) = -400 (all in kJ mole-1)
question:
Determine the lattice energy for the following reaction

Li+(g) + Cl−(g) → LiCl(s)

The given data are:

ΔHsub(Li) = 160 ; ΔHdiss(Cl2) = 244 ; IP(Li) = 520 ;

EA(Cl) = 365 and ΔHf(LiCl) = -400 (all in kJ mole-1)
solution:
For forming $1$ mole of $\text{LiCl}(s)$, the Born-Haber cycle is used.

The enthalpy of formation is for the reaction:

\text{Li}(s) + \frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{LiCl}(s)

Given:

\Delta H_f = -400 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}

We break this formation into smaller changes:

\text{Li}(s) \rightarrow \text{Li}(g)

\Delta H_{\text{sub}} = 160

\frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{Cl}(g)

Since bond dissociation of $\text{Cl}_2$ is $244$, for half mole:

\frac{244}{2} = 122

\text{Li}(g) \rightarrow \text{Li}^+(g) + e^-

IP = 520

\text{Cl}(g) + e^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^-(g)

Electron affinity releases energy, so:

EA = -365

Finally:

\text{Li}^+(g) + \text{Cl}^-(g) \rightarrow \text{LiCl}(s)

Let lattice energy be $U$.

Using Hess’s law:

\Delta H_f = \Delta H_{\text{sub}} + \frac{1}{2}\Delta H_{\text{diss}} + IP + EA + U

-400 = 160 + 122 + 520 - 365 + U

-400 = 437 + U

U = -400 - 437

U = -837 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}

So, the lattice energy for

\text{Li}^+(g) + \text{Cl}^-(g) \rightarrow \text{LiCl}(s)

is:

\boxed{-837 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}

Correct option: A.

q:
C (s) + O2 (g) → CO2 (g);   ΔH = -94.3 kcal/mol

CO (g) + $ \frac{1}{2} $ O2 (g) → CO2 (g);   ΔH = -67.4 kcal/mol

O2 (g) → 2O (g);   ΔH = 117.4 kcal/mol

CO (g) → C (g) + O (g);   ΔH = 230.6 kcal/mol

Find the value of ΔH for C (s) → C (g) in kcal/mol.
question:
C (s) + O2 (g) → CO2 (g);   ΔH = -94.3 kcal/mol

CO (g) + $ \frac{1}{2} $ O2 (g) → CO2 (g);   ΔH = -67.4 kcal/mol

O2 (g) → 2O (g);   ΔH = 117.4 kcal/mol

CO (g) → C (g) + O (g);   ΔH = 230.6 kcal/mol

Find the value of ΔH for C (s) → C (g) in kcal/mol.
solution:
We need to find $\Delta H$ for $C(s) \rightarrow C(g)$.

(1) $C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)$; $\Delta H_1 = -94.3$ kcal/mol

(2) $CO(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)$; $\Delta H_2 = -67.4$ kcal/mol

(3) $O_2(g) \rightarrow 2O(g)$; $\Delta H_3 = 117.4$ kcal/mol

(4) $CO(g) \rightarrow C(g) + O(g)$; $\Delta H_4 = 230.6$ kcal/mol

Start with equation (1): $C(s) + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2$

Reverse equation (2): $CO_2 \rightarrow CO + \frac{1}{2}O_2$; $\Delta H = +67.4$

Adding these gives: $C(s) + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow CO$; $\Delta H = -94.3 + 67.4 = -26.9$ kcal/mol

Now add equation (4): $CO \rightarrow C(g) + O(g)$; $\Delta H = 230.6$

This gives: $C(s) + \frac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow C(g) + O(g)$; $\Delta H = -26.9 + 230.6 = 203.7$ kcal/mol

To remove $O(g)$ and $\frac{1}{2}O_2$ from the equation, reverse half of equation (3):

$O(g) \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}O_2(g)$; $\Delta H = -\frac{117.4}{2} = -58.7$ kcal/mol

Adding this:

C(s) + \frac{1}{2}O_2 + O(g) \rightarrow C(g) + O(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2

C(s) \rightarrow C(g)

\Delta H = 203.7 + (-58.7) = 145 \text{ kcal/mol}

So the answer is Option D: 145 kcal/mol.

C(s) \rightarrow C(g)

So the answer is Option D: 145 kcal/mol.

q: A given quantity of ethylene on complete combustion released 5644 kJ of heat. If the heat of combustion of ethylene is 1411 kJ, then the volume of O2 (at NTP) taking part in the reaction is :
question: A given quantity of ethylene on complete combustion released 5644 kJ of heat. If the heat of combustion of ethylene is 1411 kJ, then the volume of O2 (at NTP) taking part in the reaction is :
solution:
The combustion of ethylene is:

C_2H_4 + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 2H_2O

Burning 1 mole of ethylene gives 1411 kJ of heat. Since 5644 kJ was released, the moles of ethylene burnt are:

\frac{5644}{1411} = 4 \text{ moles}

From the balanced equation, 1 mole of ethylene needs 3 moles of oxygen. So 4 moles of ethylene will need:

4 \times 3 = 12 \text{ moles of } O_2

At NTP, 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L. So the volume of oxygen used is:

12 \times 22.4 = 268.8 \text{ L}

The correct option is B.

q: When 5 liter of ethylene reacts with 5 liter of H2 gas at 1.5 atm pressure, the enthalpy change is ΔH = -0.5 kJ. The value of ΔU will be : (1 atm Lt = 100 J)
question: When 5 liter of ethylene reacts with 5 liter of H2 gas at 1.5 atm pressure, the enthalpy change is ΔH = -0.5 kJ. The value of ΔU will be : (1 atm Lt = 100 J)
solution:
The reaction is:

C_2H_4(g) + H_2(g) \rightarrow C_2H_6(g)

Here 1 mole of gas is formed from 2 moles of gas, so $\Delta n_g = -1$.

We use the relation:

\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g \, RT

But since we are dealing with actual volumes at given pressure, it's easier to use:

\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V

The volume changes from $5 + 5 = 10$ L (reactants) to $5$ L (product, since volumes are in same ratio as moles at same P and T).

So $\Delta V = 5 - 10 = -5$ L at $P = 1.5$ atm.

P\Delta V = 1.5 \times (-5) = -7.5 \text{ atm L}

Converting: $P\Delta V = -7.5 \times 100 = -750$ J $= -0.75$ kJ

Now,

\Delta U = \Delta H - P\Delta V = -0.5 - (-0.75) = 0.25 \text{ kJ}

So the answer is option C: $\Delta U = +0.25$ kJ.

So the answer is option C: $\Delta U = +0.25$ kJ.

q: For which acid-base pair is the heat of neutralization approximately $-13.6$ kcal?
question: For which acid-base pair is the heat of neutralization approximately $-13.6$ kcal?
solution:
The enthalpy of neutralization is nearly $-13.6 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}$ when a strong acid reacts with a strong base.

This is because strong acids and strong bases are completely ionised in aqueous solution. So the main reaction is simply:

\text{H}^+ (aq) + \text{OH}^- (aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)

For this reaction, the heat evolved is nearly constant:

\Delta H = -13.6 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}

Now check the options:

  • HCN is a weak acid, so Option A is not correct.

  • $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is a weak acid and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a weak base, so Option B is not correct.

  • HCl is a strong acid and KOH is a strong base, so this gives nearly $-13.6 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}$.

  • $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a weak base, so Option D is not correct.

So the correct answer is:

\boxed{\text{Option C: HCl and KOH}}

solution:

we can use Hess’s law.

Given:

\text{C(diamond)} + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2(g), \quad \Delta H = -97.6 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}

To get graphite changing into diamond, reverse the first equation:

CO_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C(diamond)} + O_2, \quad \Delta H = +97.6 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}

Now add it to the second equation:

\text{C(graphite)} + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2(g), \quad \Delta H = -94.3

CO_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C(diamond)} + O_2, \quad \Delta H = +97.6

On adding, $CO_2$ and $O_2$ cancel out:

\text{C(graphite)} \rightarrow \text{C(diamond)}

So,

\Delta H = 97.6 - 94.3 = 3.3 \text{ kcal mol}^{-1}

This is for $1$ mole of carbon, that is $12$ g of carbon.

Heat required for $1$ g carbon:

= \frac{3.3}{12}

= 0.275 \text{ kcal}

So, the correct answer is:

\boxed{0.275 \text{ kcal}}

The chemical reactions of gold were an important area of study for alchemists. Consider the reactions written below,

\begin{array}{ll} $\mathrm{Au}$ ( $\mathrm{OH}$ )_3+4 $\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ , & $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ =-28 $\mathrm{kcal}$ \\ $\mathrm{Au}$ ( $\mathrm{OH}$ )_3+4 $\mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuBr}_4+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ , & $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ =-36.8 $\mathrm{kcal}$ \end{array}

In a given experiment, 0.44 kcal of heat was absorbed when one mole of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ was mixed with 4 moles of HCl . Find the fraction of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ that changed into $\mathrm{HAuCl}_4$ (percentage conversion)
question:
The chemical reactions of gold were an important area of study for alchemists. Consider the reactions written below,

\begin{array}{ll} $\mathrm{Au}$ ( $\mathrm{OH}$ )_3+4 $\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ , & $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ =-28 $\mathrm{kcal}$ \\ $\mathrm{Au}$ ( $\mathrm{OH}$ )_3+4 $\mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuBr}_4+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ , & $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ =-36.8 $\mathrm{kcal}$ \end{array}

In a given experiment, 0.44 kcal of heat was absorbed when one mole of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ was mixed with 4 moles of HCl . Find the fraction of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ that changed into $\mathrm{HAuCl}_4$ (percentage conversion)
solution:
Using Hess’s law, first find the heat change for the conversion reaction:

\mathrm{HAuBr}_4 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4 + 4\mathrm{HBr}

Given:

\mathrm{Au(OH)}_3 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \qquad \Delta H = -28 \text{ kcal}

and

\mathrm{Au(OH)}_3 + 4\mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuBr}_4 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \qquad \Delta H = -36.8 \text{ kcal}

Reverse the second reaction:

\mathrm{HAuBr}_4 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Au(OH)}_3 + 4\mathrm{HBr} \qquad \Delta H = +36.8 \text{ kcal}

Add this to the first reaction:

\mathrm{Au(OH)}_3 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4 + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \qquad \Delta H = -28 \text{ kcal}

On cancellation, we get:

\mathrm{HAuBr}_4 + 4\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HAuCl}_4 + 4\mathrm{HBr}

The enthalpy change is:

\Delta H = 36.8 - 28 = +8.8 \text{ kcal}

So, complete conversion of $1$ mole of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ absorbs $8.8$ kcal.

But in the experiment, heat absorbed is only $0.44$ kcal.

If the fraction converted is $x$, then:

8.8x = 0.44

x = \frac{0.44}{8.8} = 0.05

So the percentage conversion is:

0.05 \times 100 = 5\%

Hence, the fraction of $\mathrm{HAuBr}_4$ converted is $0.05$, or $5\%$.

q:
Calculate the resonance energy of gaseous benzene from the given data

$\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}=416 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}}=331 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}=591 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {sub }}(\mathrm{C}$, graphite $)=718 \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {diss }}\left(\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{~g}\right)=436$ and $\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}}($ benzene, g$)=83\left(\right.$ all unit in kJ mole $\left.^{-1}\right)$
question:
Calculate the resonance energy of gaseous benzene from the given data

$\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}=416 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}}=331 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}=591 ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {sub }}(\mathrm{C}$, graphite $)=718 \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\text {diss }}\left(\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{~g}\right)=436$ and $\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}}($ benzene, g$)=83\left(\right.$ all unit in kJ mole $\left.^{-1}\right)$
solution:
To find the resonance energy, we compare the theoretical enthalpy of formation of benzene (assuming Kekulé structure with 3 single and 3 double C–C bonds) with the experimental value.

The formation reaction is:

6\,C(graphite) + 3\,H_2(g) \rightarrow C_6H_6(g)

Energy needed to convert reactants into gaseous atoms:

Sublimation of 6 C atoms:

6 \times 718 = 4308 \text{ kJ}

Dissociation of 3 H₂ molecules:

3 \times 436 = 1308 \text{ kJ}

Total energy absorbed $= 4308 + 1308 = 5616$ kJ

Now energy released when bonds form in benzene (Kekulé structure):

  • 6 C–H bonds: $6 \times 416 = 2496$ kJ

  • 3 C–C bonds: $3 \times 331 = 993$ kJ

  • 3 C=C bonds: $3 \times 591 = 1773$ kJ

Total energy released $= 2496 + 993 + 1773 = 5262$ kJ

Theoretical $\Delta H_f$ of benzene:

\Delta H_f(\text{theoretical}) = 5616 - 5262 = 354 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}

The experimental value is $83$ kJ/mol, which is lower. This extra stability is the resonance energy.

\text{Resonance energy} = \Delta H_f(\text{experimental}) - \Delta H_f(\text{theoretical})

= 83 - 354 = -271 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}

So the resonance energy of gaseous benzene is about $-271$ kJ/mol. The negative sign shows that benzene is more stable than the hypothetical Kekulé structure by $271$ kJ/mol.

q: For a 1 M solution of a weak acid, the enthalpy of neutralisation with a strong base is $-56.1 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. If the ionization enthalpy of the acid is $1.5 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and the enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base is -57.3 kJ equiv ${ }^{-1}$, find the $\%$ ionization of the weak acid in the molar solution (assume that the acid is monobasic).
question: For a 1 M solution of a weak acid, the enthalpy of neutralisation with a strong base is $-56.1 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. If the ionization enthalpy of the acid is $1.5 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and the enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base is -57.3 kJ equiv ${ }^{-1}$, find the $\%$ ionization of the weak acid in the molar solution (assume that the acid is monobasic).
solution:
Let the degree of ionization of the weak acid in $1\,\text{M}$ solution be $\alpha$.

Since the acid is monobasic, $1$ mole of acid can give $1$ mole of $\text{H}^+$ ions.

For a strong acid and strong base, the enthalpy of neutralisation is

\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}

\Delta H = -57.3\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}

For a weak acid, some part is already ionized and some part is unionized.

If $\alpha$ mole is already ionized, then $(1-\alpha)$ mole is unionized.

The unionized part must first ionize, and this needs energy:

\Delta H_{\text{ionization}} = +1.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}

So, the heat released during neutralisation of weak acid is less than that of a strong acid by the amount needed to ionize the unionized acid.

Given:

\Delta H_{\text{weak acid}} = -56.1\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}

So,

-56.1 = -57.3 + 1.5(1-\alpha)

1.5(1-\alpha) = 57.3 - 56.1

1.5(1-\alpha) = 1.2

1-\alpha = \frac{1.2}{1.5}

1-\alpha = 0.8

\alpha = 0.2

Percentage ionization:

\% \text{ ionization} = \alpha \times 100

= 0.2 \times 100

= 20\%

So, the weak acid is $20\%$ ionized in molar solution.

q:
Using the data provided, find the resonance energy of isoprene $\left(\mathrm{C}_5 \mathrm{H}_8\right)$.

It is given that $\Delta \mathrm{HC}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}=615 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}}=348 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}=413 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}=435 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$ The standard heat of sublimation of graphite is $718 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$ and the heat of formation of $\mathrm{C}_5 \mathrm{H}_8(\mathrm{~g})$ is 79 $\mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$

(Write your answer in kcal mole-1; nearest integer).
question:
Using the data provided, find the resonance energy of isoprene $\left(\mathrm{C}_5 \mathrm{H}_8\right)$.

It is given that $\Delta \mathrm{HC}_{\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}}=615 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}}=348 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}=413 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1} ; \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}=435 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$ The standard heat of sublimation of graphite is $718 \mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$ and the heat of formation of $\mathrm{C}_5 \mathrm{H}_8(\mathrm{~g})$ is 79 $\mathrm{kJmole}^{-1}$

(Write your answer in kcal mole-1; nearest integer).
solution:
For isoprene, the structure is

\mathrm{CH_2=C(CH_3)-CH=CH_2}

So the molecule contains:

  • $2$ carbon-carbon double bonds, $\mathrm{C=C}$

  • $2$ carbon-carbon single bonds, $\mathrm{C-C}$

  • $8$ carbon-hydrogen bonds, $\mathrm{C-H}$

The energy needed to form separate atoms from the elements is:

5 \times 718 + 4 \times 435

because isoprene has $5$ carbon atoms and $8$ hydrogen atoms, i.e. $4\mathrm{H_2}$ molecules.

= 3590 + 1740

= 5330 \ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

Now, if isoprene had only ordinary localized bonds, the bond energy released on formation would be:

2(\mathrm{C=C}) + 2(\mathrm{C-C}) + 8(\mathrm{C-H})

= 2(615) + 2(348) + 8(413)

= 1230 + 696 + 3304

= 5230 \ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

So the calculated heat of formation without resonance would be:

\Delta H_f = 5330 - 5230

= 100 \ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

But the given actual heat of formation is:

79 \ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

The actual molecule is more stable because of resonance. Hence resonance energy is:

100 - 79 = 21 \ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}

Converting into kcal:

\frac{21}{4.184} \approx 5 \ \mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}}

\boxed{5 \ \mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}}}

q: On complete combustion of 1 g of starch, $\left(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5\right)_x$, to form $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$, 4.6 kcal of heat is released. The heats of formation of $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$ are -94.2 and $-68.4 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{mol}$, respectively. Find the magnitude of the standard enthalpy of formation of 1 g of starch (in kcal).
question: On complete combustion of 1 g of starch, $\left(\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_5\right)_x$, to form $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$, 4.6 kcal of heat is released. The heats of formation of $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})$ are -94.2 and $-68.4 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{mol}$, respectively. Find the magnitude of the standard enthalpy of formation of 1 g of starch (in kcal).
solution:
The combustion of one repeating unit of starch is

(\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O_5}) + 6\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 6\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 5\,\mathrm{H_2O}

The molar mass of one unit $\mathrm{C_6H_{10}O_5}$ is $162$ g.

Since 1 g gives 4.6 kcal of heat, the heat released per mole (per unit) is

\Delta H_{\text{comb}} = -4.6 \times 162 = -745.2 \ \text{kcal/mol}

Using the relation

\Delta H_{\text{comb}} = \sum \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})

-745.2 = [6(-94.2) + 5(-68.4)] - \Delta H_f(\text{starch unit})

-745.2 = [-565.2 - 342.0] - \Delta H_f(\text{starch unit})

-745.2 = -907.2 - \Delta H_f(\text{starch unit})

\Delta H_f(\text{starch unit}) = -907.2 + 745.2 = -162 \ \text{kcal/mol}

So the enthalpy of formation per gram of starch is

\frac{-162}{162} = -1 \ \text{kcal/g}

The magnitude is $1$ kcal.
